title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
2 Getting Started in R

Create a new project under File - New Project. Set up a new directory for easy navigation and launch the project.
Next, create a new folder named In-class_Ex.
Inside this folder, create a subfolder named In-class_Ex01. Then, create a new Quarto document and save it in the In-class_Ex01 subfolder. Name the file In-class_Ex01.qmd.
Usually we also create another subfolder named data for storing datasets used during the analysis. Within the data folder, create three subfolders: geospatial, aspatial (attribute table), and rds for saving different types of data.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
section: 3 Installing and Loading the R packages
text:
3 Installing and Loading the R packages
There are 4 packages used in this exercise.


Package
Description



sf
Handles importing, managing, and processing vector-based geospatial data


tidyverse
A collection of R packages for data wrangling and visualisation, including readr, dplyr, and ggplot2.


tmap
Creates cartographic quality static and interactive thematic (choropleth) maps.


ggstatsplot
An extension of ggplot2.Provides graphical displays of statistical tests.


rvest
Scrapes or harvests data from web pages.



The code chunk below loads the required package into R.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, tmap, ggstatsplot, rvest)

If the required packages are not yet installed, use the function install.packages() to install them first. Remember to enclose the package names in double quotation marks (““) and separate them with commas (,) if installing more than one package.

4 Working with Master Plan Planning Sub-zone Data

As mentioned earlier, create a subfolder named data inside the In-class_Ex01 folder.
If necessary, visit data.gov.sg and download the Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) dataset from the portal in both the ESRI Shapefile and KML file formats.

The code chunk below imports the Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) dataset in both Shapefile and KML formats, and saves them as sf (simple features) data frames. Note that the import syntax differs between the two formats: when importing a Shapefile, the file extension .shp is not required, while for a KML file, the full file name including the extension must be specified in the relative directory path.

mpsz14_shp <- st_read(dsn = "data/", layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL")

section: 6 Working with Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary Data
text:
6 Working with Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary Data

6.1 Importing Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No SEA) kml
Since the MPSZ-2019 shapefile is not available yet, the following code chunk extracts the required information from the mpsz19_kml for further analysis.

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  # return NA if missing or empty
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)          #parse the HTML string 
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")  #get all table rows <tr>
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>% #keep row where <th> table header text = field_name
    html_element("td") %>%                                       #take its <td> table data
    html_text2()                                                 #extract clean text
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value        #return NA if no match, otherwise the value
}


mpsz19_kml <- mpsz19_kml %>%
  mutate(
     #for each description string, call the function, It returns a length-1 character per row (or NA)
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>% #drop the raw KML attributes
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col()) #move the geometry column to the end

6.3 Geospatial Data Wrangling

6.3.1 Point-in-Polygon Count
The code chunk below counts the number of pre-schools in each planning sub-zone. st_intersects() returns a true/false spatial relation and acts like a group_by in geometry term. The presc_list is a class of sgbp which stands for Sparse Gometry Binary Predicate. Each row corresponds to one subzone of mpsz19_kml and stores pre-school row indices in value column.

presc_list <- st_intersects(mpsz19_kml, preschool)
presc_list

The code chunk below counts the number of pre-school in each subzone and stores the counts in a new column called PreSch Count in mpsz19_kml.

mpsz19_kml <- mpsz19_kml %>%
  mutate (`PreSch Count` = lengths(
    st_intersects(mpsz19_kml, preschool)
  ))


6.3.2 Computing Density
The code chunk below derives the area of each planning sub-zone, drops the unit of measurement of the area (i.e. m^2) and calculate the density of pre-school (per km2) at the planning sub-zone level.

mpsz19_kml <- mpsz19_kml %>%
  mutate(
    Area = units::drop_units(st_area(.)),   # st_area(.) calculates the area based on the polygon geometry;
                                            # units::drop_units() removes the units class
    `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / Area * 1000000 # preschools per square kilometre
  )


6.4 Statistical Analysis
The code chunk below uses ggscatterstats() to explore and confirm the statistical relationship between Pre-school Density and Pre-school count.
ggscatterstats() checks linear association between two continuous variables and distribution of two continuous variables.
When using mpsz19_kml directly in ggscatterstats(), the error message says “x must be atomic.”
In R, atomic vectors are the basic data types: numeric, integer, character, and logical.
Non-atomic types include lists, data frames, sf geometry columns (sfc), and factors with embedded attributes.

str(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count`)

 int [1:332] 4 4 10 1 3 0 6 0 3 1 ...

str(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density`)

 num [1:332] 9.04 9.72 17.03 25.36 15.89 ...


The code chunk below drops geometry and ensures the columns are numeric, ready for ggplot.

mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density` <- as.numeric(as.character(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density`))
mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count` <- as.numeric(as.character(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count`)) 
mpsz19_kml <- as.data.frame(mpsz19_kml)

The code chunk below creates the scatter plot with Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA).

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_kml,
               x = `PreSch Count`,
               y = `PreSch Density`,
               type = "parametric")







The code chunk below creates the scatter plot under **Nonparametric” with Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA), since count is discrete and density is continuous.

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_kml,
               x = `PreSch Count`,
               y = `PreSch Density`,
               type = "nonparametric")







With 95% confidence, the Spearman correlation is 0.86 with a p-value close to 0, that confirms a strong positive association between preschool count and preschool density. This suggests that subzones with more preschools are also more likely to have higher preschool density.

z_range:       zmin: 0 zmax: 0
Projected CRS: SVY21 / Singapore TM
         Name                      geometry
52     kml_52 POINT Z (25408.32 29285.52 0)
255   kml_255 POINT Z (25579.73 29221.89 0)

1615 kml_1615 POINT Z (25867.92 29370.09 0)

mpsz19_kml$SUBZONE_N[1]

[1] "DEPOT ROAD"


The code chunk below counts the number of pre-school in each subzone and stores the counts in a new column called PreSch Count in mpsz19_kml.

mpsz19_kml <- mpsz19_kml %>%
  mutate (`PreSch Count` = lengths(
    st_intersects(mpsz19_kml, preschool)
  ))


7.1.2 Computing density
The code chunk below derives the area of each planning sub-zone, drops the unit of measurement of the area (i.e. m^2) and calculate the density of pre-school (per km2) at the planning sub-zone level.

mpsz19_kml <- mpsz19_kml %>%
  mutate(
    Area = units::drop_units(st_area(.)),   # st_area(.) calculates the area based on the polygon geometry;
                                            # units::drop_units() removes the units class
    `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / Area * 1000000 # preschools per square kilometre
  )


7.2 Statistical Analysis
The code chunk below uses ggscatterstats() to explore and confirm the statistical relationship between Pre-school Density and Pre-school count.
ggscatterstats() checks linear association between two continuous variables and distribution of two continuous variables.
When using mpsz19_kml directly in ggscatterstats(), the error message says “x must be atomic.”
In R, atomic vectors are the basic data types: numeric, integer, character, and logical.
Non-atomic types include lists, data frames, sf geometry columns (sfc), and factors with embedded attributes.

str(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count`)

 int [1:332] 4 4 10 1 3 0 6 0 3 1 ...

str(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density`)

 num [1:332] 9.04 9.72 17.03 25.36 15.89 ...


The code chunk below drops geometry and ensures the columns are numeric, ready for ggplot.

mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density` <- as.numeric(as.character(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Density`))
mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count` <- as.numeric(as.character(mpsz19_kml$`PreSch Count`)) 
mpsz19_kml <- as.data.frame(mpsz19_kml)

The code chunk below creates the scatter plot with Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA).

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_kml,
               x = `PreSch Count`,
               y = `PreSch Density`,
               type = "parametric")







The code chunk below creates the scatter plot under **Nonparametric” with Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA), since count is discrete and density is continuous.

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_kml,
               x = `PreSch Count`,
               y = `PreSch Density`,
               type = "nonparametric")







With 95% confidence, the Spearman correlation is 0.86 with a p-value close to 0, that confirms a strong positive association between preschool count and preschool density. This suggests that subzones with more preschools are also more likely to have higher preschool density.

7 Working with Population Data

7.1 Importing Data
The lastest dataset of Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling Jun 2025 can be download from Singstat homepage.
The code chunk below imports the population data into R.

popdata <- read_csv("data/respopagesextod2025.csv")
head(popdata,5)

# A tibble: 5 × 7
  PA         SZ                     AG     Sex   TOD                   Pop  Time
  <chr>      <chr>                  <chr>  <chr> <chr>               <dbl> <dbl>
1 Ang Mo Kio Ang Mo Kio Town Centre 0_to_4 Males HDB 1- and 2-Room …     0  2025
2 Ang Mo Kio Ang Mo Kio Town Centre 0_to_4 Males HDB 3-Room Flats        0  2025

4 Ang Mo Kio Ang Mo Kio Town Centre 0_to_4 Males HDB 5-Room and Exe…    10  2025
5 Ang Mo Kio Ang Mo Kio Town Centre 0_to_4 Males HUDC Flats (exclud…     0  2025



7.2 Data Wrangling
The code chunk below shows population by Planning Area and Planning subzone. summarise() is similar to group_bu and aggragrate in SQL while mutate() is like window function.

popdata2025 <- popdata %>%
         group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
        summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
        ungroup() %>%
        pivot_wider(names_from = AG,     # spreads age groups into columns
                    values_from = POP)
colnames(popdata2025)

 [1] "PA"          "SZ"          "0_to_4"      "10_to_14"    "15_to_19"   
 [6] "20_to_24"    "25_to_29"    "30_to_34"    "35_to_39"    "40_to_44"   
[11] "45_to_49"    "50_to_54"    "55_to_59"    "5_to_9"      "60_to_64"   
[16] "65_to_69"    "70_to_74"    "75_to_79"    "80_to_84"    "85_to_89"   
[21] "90_and_over"



7.3 Data Processing
The code chunk derives a tibble data.frame with the following fields PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, DEPENDENCY where by:

YOUNG: age group 0 to 4 until age groyup 20 to 24,
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age group 25-29 until age group 60-64,
AGED: age group 65 and above,
TOTAL: all age group, and
DEPENDENCY: the ratio between young and aged against economy active group.


popdata2025 <- popdata2025 %>%
  mutate(YOUNG=rowSums(.[3:6]) # Aged 0 - 24, 10 - 24
         +rowSums(.[14])) %>% # Aged 5 - 9
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(.[7:13])+ # Aged 25 - 59
  rowSums(.[15])) %>%  # Aged 60 -64
  mutate(`AGED`=rowSums(.[16:21])) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL`=rowSums(.[3:21])) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY`=(`YOUNG` + `AGED`)
  / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>% 
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, 
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`,
         `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)


7.4 Joining popdata2025 and mpsz19_kml
The code chunk blow converts the subzone and plan area to uppercase letters

popdata2025 <- popdata2025 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ),  # apply the function to these two columns: PA and SZ. mutate_at() = cross()
            .funs = list(toupper)) # #wrap the function(s) under list() and the function itself is toupper.

The code chunks below joins the subzone and population datasets together.

mpsz_pop2025 <- left_join(mpsz19_kml, popdata2025,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))


pop2025_mpsz <- left_join(popdata2025, mpsz19_kml, 
                          by = c("SZ" = "SUBZONE_N"))

The only difference is mpsz_pop2025 is data.frame and pop2025_mpsz is tbl_df. The code chunk below converts the mpsz_pop2025 back to sf object and save for futher analysis.

mpsz_pop2025 <- mpsz_pop2025 %>%
  st_as_sf()


write_rds(mpsz_pop2025,"data/mpsz_pop2025.rds")

9 Analytical Map: Percentile Map

9.1 The Concept
The percentile map is a special type of quantile map with six specific categories: 0-1%,1-10%, 10-50%,50-90%,90-99%, and 99-100%. The corresponding breakpoints can be derived by means of the base R quantile command, passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities as c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1). Note that the begin and endpoint need to be included.

9.2 Step 1: Data Preparation
The code chunk below excludes records with NA by using the code chunk below, since we notices there are a few subzones that

mpsz_pop2025 <- mpsz_pop2025 %>%
  drop_na()


sum(is.na(mpsz_pop2025[["DEPENDENCY"]]))

[1] 0



9.3 Step 2: The get Function
The code chunk below defines a function to get the input data and field to be used for creating the percentile map.

get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% 
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}


9.4 Step 3: A Percentile Mapping Function

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle=NA, mtitle="Percentile Map"){
  percent <- c(0,.01,.1,.5,.9,.99,1) # defines the breaks
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)        #  retrieve the variable 
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent) # calculates the percentile values
  tm_shape(df) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
      tm_fill(vnam,
        fill.scale = tm_scale(
        breaks = bperc,
        values = "brewer.blues",         
        value.na = NA,            
        labels = c("<1%", "1–10%", "10–50%", "50–90%", "90–99%", ">99%")),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = legtitle,        
        na.show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle)
}


9.5 Step 4: Running the functions

percentmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2025)

10 Analytical Map: Box Map

10.1 The Concept
In essence, a box map is an augmented quartile map, with an additional lower and upper category. When there are lower outliers, then the starting point for the breaks is the minimum value, and the second break is the lower fence. In contrast, when there are no lower outliers, then the starting point for the breaks will be the lower fence, and the second break is the minimum value (there will be no observations that fall in the interval between the lower fence and the minimum value).

summary(mpsz_pop2025$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.0000  0.6808  0.7445  0.7822  0.8285 13.5000 


The box plot does not tell too much about the dependency distribution.

ggplot(data = mpsz_pop2025,
       aes(x = "",
           y = DEPENDENCY)) +
  geom_boxplot()








10.2 Step 1: Creating the Boxbreaks Function
The code chunk is an R function that creating break points for a box map.

arguments:
v: vector with observations
mult: multiplier for IQR (default 1.5)
returns:
bb: vector with 7 break points compute quartile and fences


boxbreaks <- function(v,mult=1.5) {
  qv <- unname(quantile(v))
  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr
  # initialize break points vector
  bb <- vector(mode="numeric",length=7)
  # logic for lower and upper fences
  if (lofence < qv[1]) {  # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {
    bb[2] <- lofence
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
  }
  if (upfence > qv[5]) { # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]
  return(bb)
}


10.3 Step 2: Creating the get.var Function
The code chunk below creates a function to extract a variable as a vector out of an sf data frame.

arguments:
vname: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: name of sf data frame
returns:
v: vector with values (without a column name


get.var <- function(vname,df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>% st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[,1])
  return(v)
}


10.4 Step 3: Boxmap Function
The code chunk below generates an R function to create a box map.

arguments:
vnam: variable name (as character, in quotes)
df: simple features polygon layer
legtitle: legend title
mtitle: map title
mult: multiplier for IQR
returns:
a tmap-element (plots a map)


boxmap <- function(vnam, df, 
                   legtitle=NA,
                   mtitle="Box Map",
                   mult=1.5){
  var <- get.var(vnam,df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(df) +
        tm_fill(vnam,
        fill.scale = tm_scale(
        breaks = bb,
        values = "brewer.blues",         
        value.na = NA,            
        labels = c("lower outlier", 
                     "< 25%", 
                     "25% - 50%", 
                     "50% - 75%",
                     "> 75%", 
                     "upper outlier")),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = legtitle,        
        na.show = FALSE)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_layout(main.title = mtitle)
}


10.5 Step 4: Plotting Box Map

boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2025)








10.6 Plotting Interactive Box Map

tmap_mode("view")
boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2025)







tmap_mode("plot")
